title: D-R-Sh

lines: REBEKAH CAN'T MAKE SENSE OF IT.
cards: A pregnant woman feels something is wrong. The children inside her are struggling against each other, and she can't make sense of it. She says, in effect, if this is how it is, why am I?
Then she does something. Genesis says: "And she went to inquire of the LORD." That woman is Rebekah, and the verb is lidrosh, to seek, to ask, to search something out.
The same root gives Jewish tradition its word for a searching kind of reading: midrash. Dalet, resh, shin: D-R-Sh.

teach.h: THE QUESTION: REBEKAH GOES TO ASK.
teach.b: Turn this root four ways. First, the question. Rebekah doesn't wait for an answer to arrive.
She goes looking. Darash is an active verb: you get up, you go, you ask. And she gets an answer, about two nations in her womb.

teach.h: THE CALL: SEEK ME, AND LIVE.
teach.b: The prophet Amos puts it briefly, dirshuni vichyu: "Seek ye Me, and live." Seeking isn't a hobby. It's how you stay alive.
In Leviticus, Moses looks into what happened to an offering, and the text doubles the verb: darosh darash, he diligently searched.
The Talmud, in tractate Kiddushin, says these two words stand at the midpoint of the Torah's words. Some teachers love that: at the Torah's center, a man searching. Fourth, the reading.
When the rabbis read scripture, they asked why a word was spelled oddly, why a story stops where it does, why one verse sits beside another.
That seeking is called derash, and the collections of their readings are midrash, which you met on day thirty-eight, with Abram and the idols.

teach.h: THE READING: A HOUSE OF SEEKING.
teach.b: A beit midrash, a house of study, is, by its root, a house of seeking.
Midrash can be playful, daring, even surprising. It treats the text as deep enough to keep giving, and the reader as someone who has to go and ask.
So this root draws a line from a worried woman to a study hall full of arguments, both unwilling to leave a hard question alone.

how: Jews study midrash, the rabbis' interpretive readings of scripture, often in a beit midrash, a house of study, and a short teaching on the week's Torah portion is called a d'var Torah or a drash.

o: a root for seeking, and so midrash, a searching reading
a root for a road, a path walked from town to town
a root for a scroll, the parchment a scribe writes on

p: went to inquire of the LORD
a house of seeking, of study

s: midrash means reading only the surface of the text
derash seeks out what's underneath: odd spellings, gaps, neighboring verses.
the Talmud places darosh darash at the midpoint of the Torah's words
Amos's call is "seek ye Me, and live"
dirshuni vichyu, from the root D-R-Sh.

games.q: you're Rebekah. the children are struggling inside you, and you can't make sense of it. what do you do?
o: keep it to yourself and wait.
go to inquire of the LORD.
games.why: "And she went to inquire of the LORD." she seeks, and she gets an answer about two nations.

practice: Bring to mind a line you know by heart, a verse, a prayer, a lyric, something a parent used to say, and say it to yourself slowly.

Ask it one question the way the rabbis would: why this word and not another, why does it start there, what's missing? Don't rush to an answer; let the question sit beside the line, and if you pray, hold Amos's call, seek, and live.

wordCard.voice: D-R-Sh. Dalet, resh, shin: the root of darash, to seek, and of midrash, the rabbis' searching way of reading. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: midrash, a seeking-out; the rabbis' interpretive reading of scripture.

carryVoice: Your line: seek. Rebekah got up and went to ask. Until tomorrow.
